name: Pyramid training

lead: In pyramid training a lifter changes the load from set to set. An ascending pyramid adds weight and cuts reps each set; a descending pyramid starts heavy and lightens the load.

The appearance payoff is muscle: more training volume and varied loading are used to build the muscle size that shapes a physique. A 2023 review of 15 studies compared pyramid training with traditional sets.

paras: Lifters apply the scheme to compound and isolation exercises, for example building up in weight over several sets of a lift. It is mixed with straight sets and drop sets in general programmes.

Heavier sets carry the usual strength-training injury risk, and fatigue builds across sets. People with heart conditions or other health issues usually take medical advice before changing their training.

chain: Load changes across sets in a pyramid
Training volume and variety are achieved
Stimulus for muscle growth over time
angle.text: Lifters use pyramids to structure heavy and lighter sets in one exercise. Over weeks of training, that work is how they aim to add muscle that changes their physique.

lead: Pyramid training is a way of organising sets within a resistance exercise: the weight rises (ascending or crescent pyramid) or falls (descending or decrescent pyramid) from one set to the next, with repetitions moving the opposite way. A 2023 review describes it as one of the most popular methods in weight rooms.[1]

People use it as a route to muscle growth, which changes how the body looks. The review examined 15 studies (6 acute-response and 9 long-term) comparing pyramid with traditional sets on hormonal, metabolic and performance responses, strength gains and hypertrophy, and reported that pyramid training was not superior to the traditional protocol on acute physiological responses.[1]
Strength-training literature more broadly frames muscle adaptation around progressive overload, gradually increasing resistance over time.[2]

paras: In an ascending pyramid each set uses more weight and fewer repetitions; a descending pyramid reverses the order. The 2023 review searched under terms such as crescent and decrescent pyramid.[1]

The 2023 review of 15 studies rated them good to excellent in quality and found pyramid training was not superior to traditional training on acute physiological responses.[1] A randomised crossover study of 24 resistance-trained men compared drop-set, descending pyramid and traditional sets on squat, leg press and knee extension, measuring perceived exertion and pleasure/displeasure; its title reports that drop sets produced greater psychophysiological responses than pyramid and traditional sets.[3]
Pyramid-style training has also been used in cardiac rehabilitation, where a review lists it among training modalities for coronary artery disease patients.[4]
Lifters pick pyramids for variety or to ramp up before a top set. The wiki does not prescribe schemes; programme choice is individual.
